stem: Suppose a school surveys 200 students about whether they own at least one pet and whether they play a musical instrument. Let $P$ be the event that a randomly selected surveyed student owns a pet and $I$ the event that the student plays an instrument.\par\smallskip \textbf{Aaliyah:} \emph{The events overlap because 84 students do both. Since they are not mutually exclusive, they must be independent.}\par \textbf{Marcus:} \emph{Overlap does not decide independence; the relevant probabilities must be compared.}
first_take: Does owning a pet seem to change the chance that a student plays an instrument? Give one table detail in one sentence.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: State the counts for $P$, $I$, and $P\cap I$.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Find $P(I)$, $P(I\mid P)$, and $P(P\cup I)$. Show the fractions or setup.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Whose reasoning is supported? Decide independence using the two instrument-playing probabilities. Explain why the 84 students in both groups settle mutual exclusivity but do not settle independence. Write 3--4 sentences.

answers.a: There are 120 students in $P$, 100 in $I$, and 84 in $P\cap I$.
answers.c: Marcus's reasoning is supported: the events are not independent because $P(I\mid P)=0.70$ differs from $P(I)=0.50$. Knowing pet ownership changes the chance of instrument playing. The 84 students who do both show the events are not mutually exclusive, but overlap alone does not tell us whether one event changes the probability of the other.

expectedElements.description: Uses the overlap of 84 to reject mutual exclusivity
Explains why overlap and probability change answer different questions, supporting Marcus

scoringGuide.E: Includes all three required reasoning elements above, with correct contextual evidence.
scoringGuide.P: Includes at least one substantive correct reasoning link above, but omits or misstates another required element.
scoringGuide.I: Includes no substantive correct reasoning link above; an unsupported choice or copied number alone is insufficient.

commonMistakes: Comparing $P(I\mid P)$ with $P(P)$ instead of with $P(I)$
Saying events must be independent whenever both can occur
Calling owns a pet and plays an instrument mutually exclusive despite the count 84
Using $P(P)P(I)$ for the actual intersection before independence has been established
